title: SQLAlchemy and asyncpg: sessions, transactions and parameter binding
description: SQLAlchemy 2.0 Session lifecycle, async sessions, savepoints, isolation levels, psycopg and asyncpg transactions and safe parameter binding.
source: SQLAlchemy 2.0 documentation (Session basics, transactions and savepoints, asyncio extension, isolation level); psycopg 3 documentation (transactions); asyncpg documentation (transactions); PostgreSQL documentation (transaction isolation)
seriesDescription: Python and FastAPI interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Python/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Python only: nothing here mixes in Java.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: With the default expire_on_commit=True, session.commit() expires every loaded attribute, so the next attribute access reloads the row.
questions.reason: commit() discards the Session's identity map and detaches every object.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so this option wrongly calls both statements true.
whys.c: Correct: A is true; R is false because objects stay attached to the Session and are merely expired.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: In async code people set expire_on_commit=False because an expired attribute would trigger an implicit (impossible) lazy load after commit. In sync code the default is fine.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: One AsyncSession must not be shared by concurrent asyncio tasks, for example inside asyncio.gather().
questions.reason: asyncio code runs on a single operating-system thread.

whys.a: The single-thread fact does not cause the problem; interleaved awaits on one session still corrupt its state.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but the real reason is that a Session holds one transaction and one connection with mutable state.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Give each task its own session (async with session_maker() as s) or run the statements sequentially. Sessions are cheap; connections come from the pool.

questions.prompt: Given `SessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(engine)` and an ORM class User, write the async code that adds User(name="ana") in one transaction that commits when the block finishes and rolls back automatically on an exception.

checks.label: opens an async session from SessionLocal
scopes the transaction with begin() (or commits explicitly)

questions.model:
async with SessionLocal() as session:
    async with session.begin():
        session.add(User(name="ana"))
questions.explanation: `async with SessionLocal.begin() as session:` is the shorter equivalent. With an explicit `await session.commit()` you must add try/except and `await session.rollback()` yourself.

questions.prompt: With a SQLAlchemy Core connection `conn` and a Python variable `email`, run a parameterised query selecting all columns of table users where email equals the variable, using a bound parameter named :email.

checks.label: passes the value in a parameter dict
does not build the SQL with an f-string

questions.model:
result = conn.execute(
    text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email"),
    {"email": email},
)
questions.explanation: text() returns a TextClause; bound parameters are sent separately from the SQL, which prevents injection. With asyncpg the placeholder would be $1, with psycopg %s.

questions.prompt: Which psycopg call is both safe against SQL injection and syntactically correct?

options.why: Right: the driver sends the value separately; note the one-element tuple.
Python string formatting puts user input straight into the SQL text.
An f-string is still string concatenation and is injectable.

options.text: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", name)
options.why: A bare string is not a parameter sequence, so psycopg rejects it.

questions.explanation: Parameters go in a tuple or list (or a dict with %(name)s). The classic bug is forgetting the trailing comma in (name,).

questions.prompt: Match each Python data-access API with its parameter placeholder style.
questions.explanation: asyncpg uses PostgreSQL-native numbered parameters; psycopg uses %s (or %(name)s); SQLAlchemy text() uses :name; sqlite3 defaults to question marks. An f-string is never a placeholder.

questions.prompt: Using a synchronous SQLAlchemy Session named session, add Order(id=2) inside a savepoint so that a failure inside the block rolls back only that part, while Order(id=1) added earlier stays in the outer transaction.
questions.explanation: begin_nested() emits SAVEPOINT; leaving the block releases it, an exception rolls back to it. The outer transaction still needs session.commit().

questions.prompt: In one Session transaction the code adds Author A, then runs "with session.begin_nested(): add Author B; raise ValueError" inside try/except ValueError, then adds Author C and calls session.commit(). How many of A, B, C are committed?
questions.explanation: Only B is inside the savepoint, which is rolled back when the ValueError leaves the block; the caught exception does not affect the outer transaction, so A and C commit. Verified against SQLite with proper savepoint handling.

questions.prompt: Using an asyncpg connection conn, run two statements, UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1 and UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2, as one atomic transaction that commits on success and rolls back on an exception.
questions.model:
async with conn.transaction():
    await conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1")
    await conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2")
questions.explanation: The block commits when it exits normally and rolls back if an exception escapes. Nested conn.transaction() blocks become savepoints. Use $1 placeholders and pass the values instead of formatting them into the SQL.

questions.prompt: Create the SQLAlchemy engine engine for DATABASE_URL so that every connection runs at the SERIALIZABLE isolation level.
questions.explanation: Higher levels can raise serialization failures (SQLSTATE 40001) that the application must retry. engine.execution_options(isolation_level=...) or a per-connection option can change the level only where needed.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: session.flush() sends pending changes to the database inside the current transaction but does not commit them.
questions.reason: flush() emits the SQL without ending the transaction, so a later rollback() can still undo it.

whys.a: Correct: flush makes generated ids and constraint errors visible early; only commit() makes the work durable.
whys.b: Wrong: R is exactly why A holds.

questions.explanation: Use flush() when you need an auto-generated primary key before commit. commit() flushes first, so you rarely call flush() just to save data.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Using a psycopg 3 connection as a context manager commits on normal exit and rolls back when an exception leaves the block.
questions.reason: Leaving the block normally calls commit(), and leaving it with an exception calls rollback().

whys.a: Correct: R states exactly the behaviour A summarises, and the connection is closed afterwards.

questions.explanation: psycopg 3 also has conn.transaction() blocks (with savepoints when nested). In psycopg 2 the with-block ended the transaction but did not close the connection.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: PostgreSQL runs transactions at READ COMMITTED unless told otherwise.
questions.reason: PostgreSQL does not implement the REPEATABLE READ isolation level.

whys.c: Correct: A is true; R is false because PostgreSQL offers REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation) and SERIALIZABLE.

questions.explanation: Know the default of your own database: MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, PostgreSQL to READ COMMITTED.

questions.prompt: How should a FastAPI application scope its SQLAlchemy Session?

options.text: One global Session created at import time and shared by every request in the process.
options.why: Sessions are not thread-safe or task-safe; sharing leaks state between users.

options.text: One Session per request, from a Depends function that yields and closes it.
options.why: Correct: a request-scoped session keeps the identity map and transaction contained.

options.text: One Session per row inserted, committed and closed immediately.
options.why: That multiplies transactions and loses atomicity across related changes.

options.text: One Session per worker, stored on app.state, reused across requests.
options.why: It would share one transaction and identity map among concurrent requests.

questions.explanation: Engine per process, Session per request, short transactions. In async code give each task its own AsyncSession.

questions.prompt: True or false: committing after every one of 10,000 inserted rows is usually faster than inserting them all and committing once at the end.

options.why: Wrong: every commit forces a durable flush to disk, which is the expensive step.
Correct: batching many rows per transaction is much faster and keeps the work atomic.

questions.explanation: Insert in batches of a few hundred to a few thousand rows per transaction, or use bulk APIs such as executemany or COPY.

questions.prompt: Complete the SQLAlchemy 2.0 Session transaction basics.
questions.text: A Session {1} a transaction the first time it is used; call {2} to persist the changes or {3} to discard them.
questions.explanation: Using the Session as a context manager together with session.begin() commits on success and rolls back on exception automatically.
